They are up here\nrather than inside the firmware because three different things are\nbuilt from them: the firmware, the test bench, and the web app's\ncontrols.\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003cli\u003e\u003ccode\u003eAudio\u003c/code\u003e has the DSP the effects are built out of - biquads, envelope\nfollowers, LFOs - and the audio loop itself.  The bench compiles the\nsame files, so what gets measured is the pedal's own arithmetic.\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003cli\u003e\u003ccode\u003eFirmware\u003c/code\u003e is the rest of what runs on the pedal: USB, MIDI, scenes,\nthe board pin maps.\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003cli\u003e\u003ccode\u003eWebMIDI\u003c/code\u003e is the web app that edits it.\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003cli\u003e\u003ccode\u003escripts\u003c/code\u003e is what the build runs - the effect generator, the math\ntables, and the checks that refuse a firmware image doing something\nthe audio core shouldn't.\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003cli\u003e\u003ccode\u003eValidation\u003c/code\u003e is the test suite.  Some of it runs on your machine and\nsome of it wants a pedal plugged in.\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003cli\u003e\u003ccode\u003eDocumentation\u003c/code\u003e remains a very optimistic name for a directory.\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ul\u003e\n\u003cdiv class=\"markdown-heading\" dir=\"auto\"\u003e\u003ch2 tabindex=\"-1\" class=\"heading-element\" dir=\"auto\"\u003eFirmware\u003c/h2\u003e\u003ca id=\"user-content-firmware\" class=\"anchor\" aria-label=\"Permalink: Firmware\" href=\"#firmware\"\u003e\u003csvg data-component=\"Octicon\" class=\"octicon octicon-link\" viewBox=\"0 0 16 16\" version=\"1.1\" width=\"16\" height=\"16\" aria-hidden=\"true\"\u003e\u003cpath d=\"m7.775 3.275 1.25-1.25a3.5 3.5 0 1 1 4.95 4.95l-2.5 2.5a3.5 3.5 0 0 1-4.95 0 .751.751 0 0 1 .018-1.042.751.751 0 0 1 1.042-.018 1.998 1.998 0 0 0 2.83 0l2.5-2.5a2.002 2.002 0 0 0-2.83-2.83l-1.25 1.25a.751.751 0 0 1-1.042-.018.751.751 0 0 1-.018-1.042Zm-4.69 9.64a1.998 1.998 0 0 0 2.83 0l1.25-1.25a.751.751 0 0 1 1.042.018.751.751 0 0 1 .018 1.042l-1.25 1.25a3.5 3.5 0 1 1-4.95-4.95l2.5-2.5a3.5 3.5 0 0 1 4.95 0 .751.751 0 0 1-.018 1.042.751.751 0 0 1-1.042.018 1.998 1.998 0 0 0-2.83 0l-2.5 2.5a1.998 1.998 0 0 0 0 2.83Z\"\u003e\u003c/path\u003e\u003c/svg\u003e\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/div\u003e\n\u003cp dir=\"auto\"\u003eI've only ever built the firmware on Linux, but it \u003cem\u003eshould\u003c/em\u003e be perfectly\npossible to build on MacOS or Windows too if you just figure out the\nplatform requirements. The project depends on the \u003ccode\u003epico-sdk\u003c/code\u003e and\n\u003ccode\u003etinyusb\u003c/code\u003e libraries and on \u003ccode\u003epicotool\u003c/code\u003e, and has submodules for all three, so\nthey get built automatically, but the build tools your platform has to provide.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cp dir=\"auto\"\u003eRegardless of platform, you'll need the basics:\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cul dir=\"auto\"\u003e\n\u003cli\u003egit\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003cli\u003emake\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003cli\u003epython3\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003cli\u003ecmake\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003cli\u003ea C and C++ compiler for the machine you build on, because picotool\nand the SDK's PIO assembler are built from source too\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003cli\u003epkg-config and the libusb-1.0 development files, for picotool\n(\u003ccode\u003elibusb1-devel\u003c/code\u003e on Fedora, \u003ccode\u003elibusb-1.0-0-dev\u003c/code\u003e on Debian)\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ul\u003e\n\u003cp dir=\"auto\"\u003eand a 32-bit arm cross-build environment.  On Linux, that would be\nsomething like\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cul dir=\"auto\"\u003e\n\u003cli\u003earm-none-eabi-binutils-cs\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003cli\u003earm-none-eabi-gcc-cs\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003cli\u003earm-none-eabi-gcc-cs-c++ (the SDK sets up C++ as well as C)\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003cli\u003earm-none-eabi-newlib\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ul\u003e\n\u003cp dir=\"auto\"\u003eOn Fedora that whole list is\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cdiv class=\"snippet-clipboard-content notranslate position-relative overflow-auto\" data-snippet-clipboard-copy-content=\"dnf install git make python3 cmake gcc-c++ pkgconf-pkg-config \\\n    libusb1-devel arm-none-eabi-gcc-cs arm-none-eabi-gcc-cs-c++ \\\n    arm-none-eabi-newlib\"\u003e\u003cpre class=\"notranslate\"\u003e\u003ccode\u003ednf install git make python3 cmake gcc-c++ pkgconf-pkg-config \\\n    libusb1-devel arm-none-eabi-gcc-cs arm-none-eabi-gcc-cs-c++ \\\n    arm-none-eabi-newlib\n\u003c/code\u003e\u003c/pre\u003e\u003c/div\u003e\n\u003cp dir=\"auto\"\u003eThe \u003ccode\u003eble\u003c/code\u003e board also carries the nRF54 radio's firmware, which is a\nZephyr build of its own.  \u003ccode\u003emake -C nRF54 fetch\u003c/code\u003e sets that up once: a\npython venv with west in it, the Nordic SDK, and Zephyr's ARM toolchain\nin \u003ccode\u003e~/zephyr-sdk-*\u003c/code\u003e, about 7.5GB between them.  It also needs ninja\n(\u003ccode\u003eninja-build\u003c/code\u003e on Fedora).\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cp dir=\"auto\"\u003eThere's more than one board this can be built for, and the build won't\nguess.  You say which one this tree is about once, in\n\u003ccode\u003eboard.local\u003c/code\u003e, and it stays said - it's a file rather than a\ncmake cache variable specifically so that blowing away \u003ccode\u003ebuild/\u003c/code\u003e doesn't\nsilently change your mind for you.  So:\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cdiv class=\"snippet-clipboard-content notranslate position-relative overflow-auto\" data-snippet-clipboard-copy-content=\"\tgit clone https://github.com/torvalds/GuitarPedal.git\n\tcd GuitarPedal\n\techo unified \u0026gt; board.local\n\tmake prep\n\tmake\"\u003e\u003cpre class=\"notranslate\"\u003e\u003ccode\u003e\tgit clone https://github.com/torvalds/GuitarPedal.git\n\tcd GuitarPedal\n\techo unified \u0026gt; board.local\n\tmake prep\n\tmake\n\u003c/code\u003e\u003c/pre\u003e\u003c/div\u003e\n\u003cp dir=\"auto\"\u003e\u003ccode\u003eunified\u003c/code\u003e is the current one-board pedal.  The other is \u003ccode\u003esplit\u003c/code\u003e, which is\nthe older modular pair of boards.  If you forget this step the configure\nwill stop and tell you, which is the intended behaviour - a wrong board\nshould be an error you fix once, not a working build for hardware you\ndon't have.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cp dir=\"auto\"\u003eThat gets you \u003ccode\u003ebuild/pedal-unified.uf2\u003c/code\u003e (and \u003ccode\u003e.elf\u003c/code\u003e, and \u003ccode\u003e.bin\u003c/code\u003e).  Every\nartifact is named for the board it's for, so there is deliberately no\n\u003ccode\u003epedal.uf2\u003c/code\u003e to grab by mistake.  You can build the other board without\nchanging what the tree is about - \u003ccode\u003emake split\u003c/code\u003e - or both with \u003ccode\u003emake all-boards\u003c/code\u003e.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cp dir=\"auto\"\u003eTo get the \u003ccode\u003e.uf2\u003c/code\u003e onto the pedal you need it in BOOTSEL mode, and there\nare two ways.  If it's running and plugged in, send it MIDI CC 20 with\nvalue 126 and it will reboot into BOOTSEL on its own:\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cdiv class=\"snippet-clipboard-content notranslate position-relative overflow-auto\" data-snippet-clipboard-copy-content=\"\tamidi -l                          # find which card the pedal is\n\tamidi -p hw:5,0 -S \u0026quot;B0 14 7E\u0026quot;     # ...and that 5 is mine, not yours\"\u003e\u003cpre class=\"notranslate\"\u003e\u003ccode\u003e\tamidi -l                          # find which card the pedal is\n\tamidi -p hw:5,0 -S \"B0 14 7E\"     # ...and that 5 is mine, not yours\n\u003c/code\u003e\u003c/pre\u003e\u003c/div\u003e\n\u003cp dir=\"auto\"\u003eOtherwise, hold the knob in while you plug it in.  The rotary encoder's\nswitch doubles as BOOTSEL on this board - through a Schottky, so that\nQSPI traffic can't fake pulling it low - and that's the route that still\nworks on a pedal too broken to enumerate.  The older boards had a proper\nBOOTSEL button, but it was on the little MCU daughtercard, which is fine\non a bench and useless the moment the thing is screwed into a box.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cp dir=\"auto\"\u003eEither way a USB mass storage device shows up and you copy the file to\nit.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cp dir=\"auto\"\u003eThe build makes its own picotool, with USB support, so you can also skip\nall that and just do \u003ccode\u003emake flash\u003c/code\u003e, which builds and flashes the board in\n\u003ccode\u003eboard.local\u003c/code\u003e.\n\u003ccode\u003emake flash-split\u003c/code\u003e does the other one.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cdiv class=\"markdown-heading\" dir=\"auto\"\u003e\u003ch3 tabindex=\"-1\" class=\"heading-element\" dir=\"auto\"\u003eTools outside the tree\u003c/h3\u003e\u003ca id=\"user-content-tools-outside-the-tree\" class=\"anchor\" aria-label=\"Permalink: Tools outside the tree\" href=\"#tools-outside-the-tree\"\u003e\u003csvg data-component=\"Octicon\" class=\"octicon octicon-link\" viewBox=\"0 0 16 16\" version=\"1.1\" width=\"16\" height=\"16\" aria-hidden=\"true\"\u003e\u003cpath d=\"m7.775 3.275 1.25-1.25a3.5 3.5 0 1 1 4.95 4.95l-2.5 2.5a3.5 3.5 0 0 1-4.95 0 .751.751 0 0 1 .018-1.042.751.751 0 0 1 1.042-.018 1.998 1.998 0 0 0 2.83 0l2.5-2.5a2.002 2.002 0 0 0-2.83-2.83l-1.25 1.25a.751.751 0 0 1-1.042-.018.751.751 0 0 1-.018-1.042Zm-4.69 9.64a1.998 1.998 0 0 0 2.83 0l1.25-1.25a.751.751 0 0 1 1.042.018.751.751 0 0 1 .018 1.042l-1.25 1.25a3.5 3.5 0 1 1-4.95-4.95l2.5-2.5a3.5 3.5 0 0 1 4.95 0 .751.751 0 0 1-.018 1.042.751.751 0 0 1-1.042.018 1.998 1.998 0 0 0-2.83 0l-2.5 2.5a1.998 1.998 0 0 0 0 2.83Z\"\u003e\u003c/path\u003e\u003c/svg\u003e\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/div\u003e\n\u003cp dir=\"auto\"\u003eTwo tools stay outside the tree, and each has a make target that\nsets it up once per machine.  Both say what they are missing, and\nrunning either again is safe.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cp dir=\"auto\"\u003e\u003ccode\u003emake probe-rs\u003c/code\u003e builds probe-rs, which programs and debugs the nRF54\nradio through the pedal, from \u003ccode\u003e~/src/probe-rs\u003c/code\u003e into \u003ccode\u003e~/bin/probe-rs\u003c/code\u003e.\nIt needs cargo and the libudev development files (\u003ccode\u003esystemd-devel\u003c/code\u003e on\nFedora).\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cp dir=\"auto\"\u003e\u003ccode\u003emake build123d\u003c/code\u003e makes a python venv in \u003ccode\u003e~/.build123d\u003c/code\u003e for the\n3D-printed case in \u003ccode\u003eHardware/Models\u003c/code\u003e, and two commands in \u003ccode\u003e~/bin\u003c/code\u003e that\nuse it: \u003ccode\u003ebuild123d Compact.py\u003c/code\u003e runs the model, and \u003ccode\u003eocp-viewer\u003c/code\u003e is\nthe viewer it draws in, at \u003ca href=\"http://localhost:3939\" rel=\"nofollow\"\u003ehttp://localhost:3939\u003c/a\u003e.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cdiv class=\"markdown-heading\" dir=\"auto\"\u003e\u003ch3 tabindex=\"-1\" class=\"heading-element\" dir=\"auto\"\u003eTalking to the pedal without root\u003c/h3\u003e\u003ca id=\"user-content-talking-to-the-pedal-without-root\" class=\"anchor\" aria-label=\"Permalink: Talking to the pedal without can.  This is \u003ccode\u003e/etc/udev/rules.d/99-pedal.rules\u003c/code\u003e:\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cdiv class=\"snippet-clipboard-content notranslate position-relative overflow-auto\" data-snippet-clipboard-copy-content=\"ATTR{idVendor}==\u0026quot;2e8a\u0026quot;, MODE=\u0026quot;0660\u0026quot;, GROUP=\u0026quot;dialout\u0026quot;\nATTR{idVendor}==\u0026quot;ffff\u0026quot;, ATTR{idProduct}==\u0026quot;0003\u0026quot;, MODE=\u0026quot;0660\u0026quot;, GROUP=\u0026quot;dialout\u0026quot;\"\u003e\u003cpre class=\"notranslate\"\u003e\u003ccode\u003eATTR{idVendor}==\"2e8a\", MODE=\"0660\", GROUP=\"dialout\"\nATTR{idVendor}==\"ffff\", ATTR{idProduct}==\"0003\", MODE=\"0660\", GROUP=\"dialout\"\n\u003c/code\u003e\u003c/pre\u003e\u003c/div\u003e\n\u003cp dir=\"auto\"\u003eThe first line covers anything with Raspberry Pi's vendor id, which is\nhow a board in BOOTSEL shows up; the second is the running pedal, whose\nCMSIS-DAP interface is what probe-rs uses for the radio.  You have to be\nin the \u003ccode\u003edialout\u003c/code\u003e group, and \u003ccode\u003eudevadm control --reload\u003c/code\u003e as root plus a\nreplug picks the rule up.  USB audio and MIDI need no rule.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cp dir=\"auto\"\u003eThe pedal's debug console is \u003ccode\u003e/dev/ttyACM0\u003c/code\u003e, which needs a kernel with\n\u003ccode\u003eCONFIG_USB_ACM\u003c/code\u003e.  Every distribution kernel has it; a kernel you\nconfigured yourself may not.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cdiv class=\"markdown-heading\" dir=\"auto\"\u003e\u003ch3 tabindex=\"-1\" class=\"heading-element\" dir=\"auto\"\u003eTesting\u003c/h3\u003e\u003ca id=\"user-content-testing\" class=\"anchor\" aria-label=\"Permalink: Testing\" href=\"#testing\"\u003e\u003csvg data-component=\"Octicon\" class=\"octicon octicon-link\" viewBox=\"0 0 16 16\" version=\"1.1\" width=\"16\" height=\"16\" aria-hidden=\"true\"\u003e\u003cpath d=\"m7.775 3.275 1.25-1.25a3.5 3.5 0 1 1 4.95 4.95l-2.5 2.5a3.5 3.5 0 0 1-4.95 0 .751.751 0 0 1 .018-1.042.751.751 0 0 1 1.042-.018 1.998 1.998 0 0 0 2.83 0l2.5-2.5a2.002 2.002 0 0 0-2.83-2.83l-1.25 1.25a.751.751 0 0 1-1.042-.018.751.751 0 0 1-.018-1.042Zm-4.69 9.64a1.998 1.998 0 0 0 2.83 0l1.25-1.25a.751.751 0 0 1 1.042.018.751.751 0 0 1 .018 1.042l-1.25 1.25a3.5 3.5 0 1 1-4.95-4.95l2.5-2.5a3.5 3.5 0 0 1 4.95 0 .751.751 0 0 1-.018 1.042.751.751 0 0 1-1.042.018 1.998 1.998 0 0 0-2.83 0l-2.5 2.5a1.998 1.998 0 0 0 0 2.83Z\"\u003e\u003c/path\u003e\u003c/svg\u003e\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/div\u003e\n\u003cp dir=\"auto\"\u003e\u003ccode\u003eValidation\u003c/code\u003e has the test suite, and it's split by what it needs.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cp dir=\"auto\"\u003e\u003ccode\u003emake check\u003c/code\u003e needs gcc and numpy (\u003ccode\u003epython3-numpy\u003c/code\u003e), plus node if\nyou want the web app's tests too; without node those are skipped.  The\nbench scripts that talk to a pedal want more: alsa-utils, ffmpeg, scipy\nand matplotlib, ngspice for the circuit comparisons, and dbus-python and\nPyGObject for Bluetooth MIDI.  On Fedora,\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cdiv class=\"snippet-clipboard-content notranslate position-relative overflow-auto\" data-snippet-clipboard-copy-content=\"dnf install python3-numpy nodejs alsa-utils ffmpeg-free psmisc \\\n    python3-scipy python3-matplotlib ngspice python3-dbus python3-gobject\"\u003e\u003cpre class=\"notranslate\"\u003e\u003ccode\u003ednf install python3-numpy nodejs alsa-utils ffmpeg-free psmisc \\\n    python3-scipy python3-matplotlib ngspice python3-dbus python3-gobject\n\u003c/code\u003e\u003c/pre\u003e\u003c/div\u003e\n\u003cp dir=\"auto\"\u003e\u003ccode\u003emake check\u003c/code\u003e runs the part that needs no hardware at all: the MIDI\npacketiser, whether the web app still loads and still draws the right\nconclusions, and a sweep that asks every biquad in the pedal where it\nactually landed.  \u003ccode\u003emake check-biquad\u003c/code\u003e is that last one on its own, and\n\u003ccode\u003emake check-effects\u003c/code\u003e puts signals through the effects themselves.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cp dir=\"auto\"\u003eThat last one works because of \u003ccode\u003eValidation/bench\u003c/code\u003e, which builds the\npedal's actual audio core - the same \u003ccode\u003esingle_sample()\u003c/code\u003e, the same effect\nheaders, the same compiler flags - as a program on your machine that\ntakes float samples on stdin and hands them back on stdout.  It is not a\nmodel of the signal path.  It's the signal path, with the two register\nblocks the audio core touches replaced by ordinary memory.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cp dir=\"auto\"\u003e\u003ccode\u003emake check-analysis\u003c/code\u003e is the other host-only one, and it is what keeps\nthe per-effect pages under \u003ccode\u003eDocumentation/effects\u003c/code\u003e honest: every curve on\nthose pages is a measurement, and this re-measures and says when one has\nstopped being true.  It is separate from \u003ccode\u003echeck\u003c/code\u003e because it re-runs\nevery sweep on every page, which is slow.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cp dir=\"auto\"\u003eThen there are the ones that want hardware: \u003ccode\u003emake check-hw\u003c/code\u003e with a\nsignal generator, \u003ccode\u003emake check-analog\u003c/code\u003e with a patch cable from the\npedal's output back to its own input, \u003ccode\u003emake check-bench\u003c/code\u003e to ask whether\na real board agrees with the host build, \u003ccode\u003emake check-hwtone\u003c/code\u003e to sweep\nthe tone stack the codec runs in its own biquads, and \u003ccode\u003emake check-loop\u003c/code\u003e\nif you have two pedals to patch into each other.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cdiv class=\"markdown-heading\" dir=\"auto\"\u003e\u003ch2 enclosure drill rules) are in the \u003ccode\u003eHardware\u003c/code\u003e\nsubdirectory.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cp dir=\"auto\"\u003eThese days it's just the one board.  \u003ccode\u003eHardware/usb-stomp\u003c/code\u003e has the RP2354A\nand the TI TAC5242 codec sitting directly on it, and that's the whole\npedal: no cable, no daughtercards, no connectors in between.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cp dir=\"auto\"\u003eWhat's on it:\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cul dir=\"auto\"\u003e\n\u003cli\u003ea 1/4\" input jack and a 1/4\" output jack\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003cli\u003ea third 1/4\" jack for an expression pedal or a remote stomp switch\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003cli\u003eMIDI in and out, on 3.5mm \"Type A\" TRS jacks (out through a 5V\nbuffer, in through an optocoupler, like MIDI has always wanted)\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003cli\u003eUSB-C, and the usual 9V guitar pedal power jack\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003cli\u003eone rotary encoder with a switch under it, and one stomp switch\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003cli\u003ethree addressable WS2812B LEDs\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ul\u003e\n\u003cp dir=\"auto\"\u003eThe MIDI jacks and the expression jack are the genuinely new things.  The\nolder boards had nowhere to put them - the expression jack in particular\nwants two ADC pins, and those are exactly the pins the old MCU board was\nspending on hardware MIDI, so it could not have existed there at all.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cp dir=\"auto\"\u003eFair warning on that expression jack, though: the hardware is done and\nthe firmware can read it, but only when the host asks it to over SysEx.\nRight now it's a probe for figuring out what people actually plug in\nthere - expression pedals don't even agree on which contact is the wiper\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cul dir=\"auto\"\u003e\n\u003cli\u003eand nothing is wired up to \u003cem\u003edo\u003c/em\u003e anything with the result yet.\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ul\u003e\n\u003cdiv class=\"markdown-heading\" dir=\"auto\"\u003e\u003ch3 tabindex=\"-1\" class=\"heading-element\" dir=\"auto\"\u003eHow it used to be\u003c/h3\u003e\u003ca id=\"user-content-how-it-used-to-be\" class=\"anchor\" aria-label=\"Permalink: How it used to be\" href=\"#how-it-used-to-be\"\u003e\u003csvg data-component=\"Octicon\" class=\"octicon octicon-link\" viewBox=\"0 0 16 16\" version=\"1.1\" width=\"16\" height=\"16\" aria-hidden=\"true\"\u003e\u003cpath d=\"m7.775 3.275 1.25-1.25a3.5 3.5 0 1 1 4.95 4.95l-2.5 2.5a3.5 3.5 0 0 1-4.95 0 .751.751 0 0 1 .018-1.042.751.751 0 0 1 1.042-.018 1.998 1.998 0 0 0 2.83 0l2.5-2.5a2.002 2.002 0 0 0-2.83-2.83l-1.25 1.25a.751.751 0 0 1-1.042-.018.751.751 0 0 1-.018-1.042Zm-4.69 9.64a1.998 1.998 0 0 0 2.83 0l1.25-1.25a.751.751 0 0 1 1.042.018.751.751 0 0 1 .018 1.042l-1.25 1.25a3.5 3.5 0 1 1-4.95-4.95l2.5-2.5a3.5 3.5 0 0 1 4.95 0 .751.751 0 0 1-.018 1.042.751.751 0 0 1-1.042.018 1.998 1.998 0 0 0-2.83 0l-2.5 2.5a1.998 1.998 0 0 0 0 2.83Z\"\u003e\u003c/path\u003e\u003c/svg\u003e\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/div\u003e\n\u003cp dir=\"auto\"\u003eIt used to be modular, and those board files are all still here.  There\nwere two little daughtercards for the \"core\" hardware - the RP2354\nmicrocontroller (\u003ccode\u003eHardware/rp2354\u003c/code\u003e) and the TI TAC5112 codec\n(\u003ccode\u003eHardware/codec\u003c/code\u003e) - plus a board for the audio and 9V DC power jacks\n(\u003ccode\u003eHardware/audio-jacks\u003c/code\u003e), and a main board (\u003ccode\u003eHardware/pedal-board\u003c/code\u003e) for\nthe pedal IO: i2c connector for the screen, USB-C programming port,\nrotary encoders, pin header for stomp switches.  The two halves were\njoined by a 12P 0.5mm FFC cable carrying power and data lines (i2c for\ncontrol, i2s for audio).\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cp dir=\"auto\"\u003eThat was mostly so I could try out different form factors.  It let me lay\nthe two halves out independently, and it was flexible enough to cram a\n125B enclosure full of jacks, rotaries and the screen all in one top\narea.  There was also a worry about noise isolation, which in the end\nnever had to be tested.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cp dir=\"auto\"\u003eI used the nice HiRose BM28 series connectors on the modular boards.\nThey are absolutely tiny, which makes for a great board footprint but\nadmittedly also makes for a slightly more complicated board due to the\ntiny 0.35mm pitch.  I'm not a fan of the traditional pin headers simply\nbecause they make it so hard to do compact form factors.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cp dir=\"auto\"\u003eThose boards are finished and they still work - the firmware builds for\nthem, and they're still useful for testing.  But what this section used\nto say was that if you know what you want, you should just put the codec\ndirectly on the audio jack board and the rp2354 on the IO board.  Which,\nyes.  That's the board above.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cdiv class=\"markdown-heading\" dir=\"auto\"\u003e\u003ch3 tabindex=\"-1\" class=\"heading-element\" dir=\"auto\"\u003eImages\u003c/h3\u003e\u003ca 2.83Z\"\u003e\u003c/path\u003e\u003c/svg\u003e\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/div\u003e\n\u003cp dir=\"auto\"\u003eThere's no screen.  The pedal has one knob, one footswitch and three\nLEDs, and everything else happens in a browser.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cdiv class=\"markdown-heading\" dir=\"auto\"\u003e\u003ch3 tabindex=\"-1\" class=\"heading-element\" dir=\"auto\"\u003eOn the pedal\u003c/h3\u003e\u003ca id=\"user-content-on-the-pedal\" class=\"anchor\" aria-label=\"Permalink: On the pedal\" href=\"#on-the-pedal\"\u003e\u003csvg data-component=\"Octicon\" class=\"octicon octicon-link\" viewBox=\"0 0 16 16\" version=\"1.1\" width=\"16\" height=\"16\" aria-hidden=\"true\"\u003e\u003cpath d=\"m7.775 3.275 1.25-1.25a3.5 3.5 0 1 1 4.95 4.95l-2.5 2.5a3.5 3.5 0 0 1-4.95 0 .751.751 0 0 1 .018-1.042.751.751 0 0 1 1.042-.018 1.998 1.998 0 0 0 2.83 0l2.5-2.5a2.002 2.002 0 0 0-2.83-2.83l-1.25 1.25a.751.751 0 0 1-1.042-.018.751.751 0 0 1-.018-1.042Zm-4.69 9.64a1.998 1.998 0 0 0 2.83 0l1.25-1.25a.751.751 0 0 1 1.042.018.751.751 0 0 1 .018 1.042l-1.25 1.25a3.5 3.5 0 1 1-4.95-4.95l2.5-2.5a3.5 3.5 0 0 1 4.95 0 .751.751 0 0 1-.018 1.042.751.751 0 0 1-1.042.018 1.998 1.998 0 0 0-2.83 0l-2.5 2.5a1.998 1.998 0 0 0 0 2.83Z\"\u003e\u003c/path\u003e\u003c/svg\u003e\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/div\u003e\n\u003cp dir=\"auto\"\u003eOut of the box the footswitch is bypass - tap for in-circuit or not, hold\nit for the tuner - and the knob is the master volume, with either kind of\npress on it putting the volume back where it started.  That last one\nsounds trivial and isn't: it's the way back when you can't see anything.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cp dir=\"auto\"\u003eBut none of that is compiled in.  There are five gestures - turn the\nknob, tap it, hold it, tap the switch, hold the switch - and what each\none means is a table the pedal looks up and the app writes.  You can\npoint the knob at any parameter of any effect, or make a single press\ntake one effect's mix up while it takes another's down.  A pedal with no\nscreen can't tell you what its knob is for, so that has to be settable\nfrom something that can.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cp dir=\"auto\"\u003eThe three LEDs, left to right: something is wrong (red for clipping,\namber for dropped samples), in circuit or bypassed, and the chain is\nbusy - where \"busy\" means whatever the effect thinks it means, so the\ngate lights it while it's gating and the compressor while it's\ncompressing.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cdiv class=\"markdown-heading\" dir=\"auto\"\u003e\u003ch3 tabindex=\"-1\" class=\"heading-element\" dir=\"auto\"\u003eIn the browser\u003c/h3\u003e\u003ca id=\"user-content-in-the-browser\" class=\"anchor\" aria-label=\"Permalink: In the browser\" href=\"#in-the-browser\"\u003e\u003csvg data-component=\"Octicon\" class=\"octicon octicon-link\" viewBox=\"0 0 16 16\" version=\"1.1\" width=\"16\" height=\"16\" aria-hidden=\"true\"\u003e\u003cpath d=\"m7.775 3.275 1.25-1.25a3.5 3.5 0 1 1 4.95 4.95l-2.5 2.5a3.5 3.5 0 0 1-4.95 0 .751.751 0 0 1 .018-1.042.751.751 0 0 1 1.042-.018 1.998 1.998 0 0 0 2.83 0l2.5-2.5a2.002 2.002 0 0 0-2.83-2.83l-1.25 1.25a.751.751 0 0 1-1.042-.018.751.751 0 0 1-.018-1.042Zm-4.69 9.64a1.998 1.998 0 0 0 2.83 0l1.25-1.25a.751.751 0 0 1 1.042.018.751.751 0 0 1 .018 1.042l-1.25 1.25a3.5 3.5 0 1 1-4.95-4.95l2.5-2.5a3.5 3.5 0 0 1 4.95 0 .751.751 0 0 1-.018 1.042.751.751 0 0 1-1.042.018 1.998 1.998 0 0 0-2.83 0l-2.5 2.5a1.998 1.998 0 0 0 0 2.83Z\"\u003e\u003c/path\u003e\u003c/svg\u003e\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/div\u003e\n\u003cp dir=\"auto\"\u003e\u003ccode\u003eWebMIDI\u003c/code\u003e is a static web page that talks to the pedal over USB\nMIDI.  There's nothing to install and it runs off a phone.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cp dir=\"auto\"\u003eIt also talks to the pedal over Bluetooth MIDI.  On Linux, Chrome only\noffers Bluetooth to a page with\n\u003ccode\u003echrome://flags/#enable-experimental-web-platform-features\u003c/code\u003e turned on;\nUSB needs nothing.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cp dir=\"auto\"\u003eIt doesn't know what the effects are.  It asks.  The pedal describes\nevery effect it has - every pot, the ranges, the units, the hover text -\nand the app builds itself out of that, so it can't drift out of step with\nthe firmware, and adding an effect to the pedal makes it show up in the\napp without touching the app.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cp dir=\"auto\"\u003eWhat you actually do there is \u003cem\u003eroute\u003c/em\u003e.  There are seventeen effects and\nnone of them are in your signal path until you say so: routing picks\nwhich ones run, and in what order, and the order is yours, because a\nboost in front of a delay is a different pedal from a delay in front of a\nboost.  Whatever you don't route costs nothing.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cp dir=\"auto\"\u003ePots are mostly just numbers, except where they aren't - the tone stacks,\nthe parametric EQ and the cab sim draw their actual frequency response,\nso you can see the curve instead of inferring it from three knob\npositions.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cp dir=\"auto\"\u003e\u003ca target=\"_blank\" rel=\"noopener noreferrer\" href=\"/torvalds/GuitarPedal/blob/main/Images/WebMIDI-screenshot.png\"\u003e\u003cimg src=\"/torvalds/GuitarPedal/raw/main/Images/WebMIDI-screenshot.png\" width=\"420\" alt=\"The WebMIDI app with a tone control and a tape echo routed\" style=\"max-width: 100%;\"\u003e\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cp dir=\"auto\"\u003eA tone stack with a 10dB mid bump at 810Hz and a tape echo behind it, and\nthe fifteen effects that aren't routed sitting at the bottom waiting to\nbe.  The faint grey line is the phase response.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cp dir=\"auto\"\u003eEight scenes fit in the pedal's own flash.  A scene is a routing plus\neverything set inside it, and a MIDI program change recalls one, which is\nhalf of what those MIDI jacks are for: a cheap footswitch can step\nbetween scenes with no computer in sight.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cdiv class=\"markdown-heading\" dir=\"auto\"\u003e\u003ch2 tabindex=\"-1\" class=\"heading-element\" dir=\"auto\"\u003eAudio effects\u003c/h2\u003e\u003ca 0 16 16\" version=\"1.1\" width=\"16\" height=\"16\" aria-hidden=\"true\"\u003e\u003cpath d=\"m7.775 3.275 1.25-1.25a3.5 3.5 0 1 1 4.95 4.95l-2.5 2.5a3.5 3.5 0 0 1-4.95 0 .751.751 0 0 1 0l1.25-1.25a.751.751 0 0 1 1.042.018.751.751 0 0 1 .018 1.042l-1.25 1.25a3.5 3.5 0 1 1-4.95-4.95l2.5-2.5a3.5 3.5 0 0 1 4.95 0 .751.751 0 0 1-.018 1.042.751.751 0 0 1-1.042.018 1.998 1.998 0 0 0-2.83 0l-2.5 2.5a1.998 1.998 0 0 0 0 2.83Z\"\u003e\u003c/path\u003e\u003c/svg\u003e\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/div\u003e\n\u003cp dir=\"auto\"\u003eNineteen of them, plus five that are always there and can't be\nunrouted: the \u003cstrong\u003eSignal Chain\u003c/strong\u003e at the front, which is the input trim, the\nnoise gate and the master volume\n(\u003ca href=\"/torvalds/GuitarPedal/blob/main/Documentation/effects/signal-chain.md\"\u003emeasured\u003c/a\u003e), and behind them the\n\u003cstrong\u003eSettings\u003c/strong\u003e, which is whether the input jack is carrying one channel or\ntwo, the MIDI channel, LED brightness and what the tuner is tuning to,\nthe \u003cstrong\u003eUSB Audio\u003c/strong\u003e, which is what crosses the wire in each direction, the\n\u003cstrong\u003eBluetooth Audio\u003c/strong\u003e, which is where audio from a phone joins, how loud it\nis and what goes back, on a board with a radio, and the \u003cstrong\u003eExpression Jack\u003c/strong\u003e, which is what\nis plugged into it and where that thing's travel ends.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cp dir=\"auto\"\u003eThey're listed in the order they run in by default.  This is an overview\nand not documentation - the app is the reference, because it gets the\nranges, the units and the hover text from the pedal itself rather than\nfrom anything I typed here.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cul dir=\"auto\"\u003e\n\u003cli\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eHum Filter\u003c/strong\u003e - removes the hum single coils and noisy power put on\nthe guitar, cutting only the hum's own frequencies, so a clean supply\ngets no cuts at all.  Switching it on the first time, or moving the\ntarget, listens for a few seconds with the sound left on, so you hear\nthe hum go: keep the strings quiet while it does.  It runs ahead of\nthe noise gate.  It does not reach the high buzz some USB chargers\nadd, and a power bank is quieter there anyway.\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003cli\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eTone\u003c/strong\u003e - bass, mid and treble, with the corner frequencies\nadjustable and the mid's Q as well.  There are two of them, so one\ncan go in front of a distortion and one behind it.\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003cli\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eAnalog In Tone\u003c/strong\u003e and \u003cstrong\u003eAnalog Out Tone\u003c/strong\u003e - the same three bands\nagain, running in the codec's own biquads rather than in the chain.\nThey cost the audio core nothing, and they keep the two channels\napart where Tone folds them together.  Routed like anything\nelse, but drawn at the ends of the chain because that is where they\nare: analog is the operative word, and they sit outside everything\nUSB audio can reach, so a Dry capture has already been through the\ninput one and a Wet capture has not yet been through the output one.\nThey need a board whose codec answers on i2c.\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003cli\u003e\u003cstrong\u003ePreamp\u003c/strong\u003e - a two-stage 12AX7 model, class-A biased with the\nasymmetry left in, and a JFET stage after it.\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003cli\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eCompressor\u003c/strong\u003e - level, ratio, attack, release, and a boost, so it\ncan also just be a clean boost when that's what you want.  The\nthreshold reaches low enough to work on a quiet pickup with nothing\nin front of it.  \u003ca href=\"/torvalds/GuitarPedal/blob/main/Documentation/effects/compressor.md\"\u003eMeasured\u003c/a\u003e.\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003cli\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eAuto-Wah\u003c/strong\u003e - an envelope filter that sweeps a resonant filter with\nthe guitar's pick dynamics, by Jacky Mpoka.  Lowpass mode preserves low-end body while\nsweeping harmonics (Mu-Tron III style); Bandpass mode isolates the\nresonant peak for classic vocal wah (Crybaby style).  Sweeps up for\nfunk quack or down for synth sweeps.\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003cli\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eBoost\u003c/strong\u003e, with distortion.  I like this one.  Others may not.  Set\nthe boost stupidly high and the level low, and instead of clipping at\nthe level the signal \u003cem\u003efolds\u003c/em\u003e back down, which gives you harmonics\nthat a soft or hard clipper doesn't.\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003cli\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eKlonlike\u003c/strong\u003e - the obvious model: 18V charge pump for headroom,\ngermanium diodes, and the clean/dirty blend that tracks the gain\nknob.  Originally by Bryan Leavelle.\n\u003ca href=\"/torvalds/GuitarPedal/blob/main/Documentation/effects/klon.md\"\u003eMeasured\u003c/a\u003e.\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003cli\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eRat Sketch\u003c/strong\u003e - a ProCo RAT, from the Aion FX Helios clone.  One\nop-amp with up to 67dB and several decibels an octave of treble\nemphasis inside the feedback, then diodes to ground, then the one\nbackwards Filter knob.  Three clipping modes, because the pedal has\nthree.  The op-amp saturates inside its own loop and the diodes are\nsolved rather than approximated, which is where its second harmonic\ncomes from.  \u003ca href=\"/torvalds/GuitarPedal/blob/main/Documentation/effects/rat.md\"\u003eMeasured\u003c/a\u003e.\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003cli\u003e\u003cstrong\u003ePhaser\u003c/strong\u003e, \u003cstrong\u003eFlanger\u003c/strong\u003e and \u003cstrong\u003eVibrato\u003c/strong\u003e - the modulation three.  All\nsimple, all a delay line and an LFO wearing different hats.\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003cli\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eTape Echo\u003c/strong\u003e - the Echo King from Cleveland Music Co, a model of the\nMaestro Echoplex tape delays, converted from the Hothouse examples.\nAll credit to Ricky Sheaves, and blame me for the conversion.\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003cli\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eReverb\u003c/strong\u003e - comb filters into allpasses, the traditional way.\n\u003ca href=\"/torvalds/GuitarPedal/blob/main/Documentation/effects/reverb.md\"\u003eMeasured\u003c/a\u003e.\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003cli\u003e\u003cstrong\u003ePitch\u003c/strong\u003e - not the clever FFT kind.  It walks a delay line faster or\nslower than real time in two phases, crossfaded with a sine so the\nwrap doesn't click.  So it shifts \u003cem\u003eand\u003c/em\u003e delays, and it feeds back into\nitself, which makes it a short echo that shifts again on every repeat.\nMost natural an octave up, but it does fractions.\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003cli\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eTremolo\u003c/strong\u003e - amplitude modulation, several shapes.\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003cli\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eParametric EQ\u003c/strong\u003e - five bands, two shelves and three peaks, every one\nof them tunable across the whole range.\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003cli\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eFrenchie Amp\u003c/strong\u003e - a small amp: triode, tone stack, power amp.\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003cli\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eTest Tone\u003c/strong\u003e - sine, triangle, saw or noise at a known level and\nfrequency. <p dir="auto">This is a resurrected version of my old guitar pedal project: a digital
guitar pedal built around an RP2354A and a TI audio codec, with all the
effects done in software on a core of its own.</p>
<p dir="auto">It went through a phase with a little OLED screen and a couple of rotary
encoders on it, and that's gone now.  Editing seventeen effects through a
128x128 screen and two knobs was never going to be pleasant, and I'm not
exactly known for my mad UI designing skillz, so the pedal itself is down
to one knob and one stomp switch and the deep editing happens somewhere
that already has a screen: there's a web app that talks to it over USB
MIDI from a browser.</p>
<p dir="auto">So what's in here:</p>
<ul dir="auto">
<li><code>Hardware</code> has the kicad files.</li>
<li><code>Effects</code> has the seventeen effects, one file each.  They are up here
rather than inside the firmware because three different things are
built from them: the firmware, the test bench, and the web app's
controls.</li>
<li><code>Audio</code> has the DSP the effects are built out of - biquads, envelope
followers, LFOs - and the audio loop itself.  The bench compiles the
same files, so what gets measured is the pedal's own arithmetic.</li>
<li><code>Firmware</code> is the rest of what runs on the pedal: USB, MIDI, scenes,
the board pin maps.</li>
<li><code>WebMIDI</code> is the web app that edits it.</li>
<li><code>scripts</code> is what the build runs - the effect generator, the math
tables, and the checks that refuse a firmware image doing something
the audio core shouldn't.</li>
<li><code>Validation</code> is the test suite.  Some of it runs on your machine and
some of it wants a pedal plugged in.</li>
<li><code>Documentation</code> remains a very optimistic name for a directory.</li>
</ul>
<div class="markdown-heading" dir="auto"><h2 tabindex="-1" class="heading-element" dir="auto">Firmware</h2><a id="user-content-firmware" class="anchor" aria-label="Permalink: Firmware" href="#firmware"><svg data-component="Octicon" class="octicon octicon-link" viewBox="0 0 16 16" version="1.1" width="16" height="16" aria-hidden="true"><path d="m7.775 3.275 1.25-1.25a3.5 3.5 0 1 1 4.95 4.95l-2.5 2.5a3.5 3.5 0 0 1-4.95 0 .751.751 0 0 1 .018-1.042.751.751 0 0 1 1.042-.018 1.998 1.998 0 0 0 2.83 0l2.5-2.5a2.002 2.002 0 0 0-2.83-2.83l-1.25 1.25a.751.751 0 0 1-1.042-.018.751.751 0 0 1-.018-1.042Zm-4.69 9.64a1.998 1.998 0 0 0 2.83 0l1.25-1.25a.751.751 0 0 1 1.042.018.751.751 0 0 1 .018 1.042l-1.25 1.25a3.5 3.5 0 1 1-4.95-4.95l2.5-2.5a3.5 3.5 0 0 1 4.95 0 .751.751 0 0 1-.018 1.042.751.751 0 0 1-1.042.018 1.998 1.998 0 0 0-2.83 0l-2.5 2.5a1.998 1.998 0 0 0 0 2.83Z"></path></svg></a></div>
<p dir="auto">I've only ever built the firmware on Linux, but it <em>should</em> be perfectly
possible to build on MacOS or Windows too if you just figure out the
platform requirements. The project depends on the <code>pico-sdk</code> and
<code>tinyusb</code> libraries and on <code>picotool</code>, and has submodules for all three, so
they get built automatically, but the build tools your platform has to provide.</p>
<p dir="auto">Regardless of platform, you'll need the basics:</p>
<ul dir="auto">
<li>git</li>
<li>make</li>
<li>python3</li>
<li>cmake</li>
<li>a C and C++ compiler for the machine you build on, because picotool
and the SDK's PIO assembler are built from source too</li>
<li>pkg-config and the libusb-1.0 development files, for picotool
(<code>libusb1-devel</code> on Fedora, <code>libusb-1.0-0-dev</code> on Debian)</li>
</ul>
<p dir="auto">and a 32-bit arm cross-build environment.  On Linux, that would be
something like</p>
<ul dir="auto">
<li>arm-none-eabi-binutils-cs</li>
<li>arm-none-eabi-gcc-cs</li>
<li>arm-none-eabi-gcc-cs-c++ (the SDK sets up C++ as well as C)</li>
<li>arm-none-eabi-newlib</li>
</ul>
<p dir="auto">On Fedora that whole list is</p>
<div class="snippet-clipboard-content notranslate position-relative overflow-auto" data-snippet-clipboard-copy-content="dnf install git make python3 cmake gcc-c++ pkgconf-pkg-config \
    libusb1-devel arm-none-eabi-gcc-cs arm-none-eabi-gcc-cs-c++ \
    arm-none-eabi-newlib"><pre class="notranslate"><code>dnf install git make python3 cmake gcc-c++ pkgconf-pkg-config \
    libusb1-devel arm-none-eabi-gcc-cs arm-none-eabi-gcc-cs-c++ \
    arm-none-eabi-newlib
</code></pre></div>
<p dir="auto">The <code>ble</code> board also carries the nRF54 radio's firmware, which is a
Zephyr build of its own.  <code>make -C nRF54 fetch</code> sets that up once: a
python venv with west in it, the Nordic SDK, and Zephyr's ARM toolchain
in <code>~/zephyr-sdk-*</code>, about 7.5GB between them.  It also needs ninja
(<code>ninja-build</code> on Fedora).</p>
<p dir="auto">There's more than one board this can be built for, and the build won't
guess.  You say which one this tree is about once, in
<code>board.local</code>, and it stays said - it's a file rather than a
cmake cache variable specifically so that blowing away <code>build/</code> doesn't
silently change your mind for you.  So:</p>
<div class="snippet-clipboard-content notranslate position-relative overflow-auto" data-snippet-clipboard-copy-content="	git clone https://github.com/torvalds/GuitarPedal.git
	cd GuitarPedal
	echo unified > board.local
	make prep
	make"><pre class="notranslate"><code>	git clone https://github.com/torvalds/GuitarPedal.git
	cd GuitarPedal
	echo unified > board.local
	make prep
	make
</code></pre></div>
<p dir="auto"><code>unified</code> is the current one-board pedal.  The other is <code>split</code>, which is
the older modular pair of boards.  If you forget this step the configure
will stop and tell you, which is the intended behaviour - a wrong board
should be an error you fix once, not a working build for hardware you
don't have.</p>
<p dir="auto">That gets you <code>build/pedal-unified.uf2</code> (and <code>.elf</code>, and <code>.bin</code>).  Every
artifact is named for the board it's for, so there is deliberately no
<code>pedal.uf2</code> to grab by mistake.  You can build the other board without
changing what the tree is about - <code>make split</code> - or both with <code>make all-boards</code>.</p>
<p dir="auto">To get the <code>.uf2</code> onto the pedal you need it in BOOTSEL mode, and there
are two ways.  If it's running and plugged in, send it MIDI CC 20 with
value 126 and it will reboot into BOOTSEL on its own:</p>
<div class="snippet-clipboard-content notranslate position-relative overflow-auto" data-snippet-clipboard-copy-content="	amidi -l                          # find which card the pedal is
	amidi -p hw:5,0 -S "B0 14 7E"     # ...and that 5 is mine, not yours"><pre class="notranslate"><code>	amidi -l                          # find which card the pedal is
	amidi -p hw:5,0 -S "B0 14 7E"     # ...and that 5 is mine, not yours
</code></pre></div>
<p dir="auto">Otherwise, hold the knob in while you plug it in.  The rotary encoder's
switch doubles as BOOTSEL on this board - through a Schottky, so that
QSPI traffic can't fake pulling it low - and that's the route that still
works on a pedal too broken to enumerate.  The older boards had a proper
BOOTSEL button, but it was on the little MCU daughtercard, which is fine
on a bench and useless the moment the thing is screwed into a box.</p>
<p dir="auto">Either way a USB mass storage device shows up and you copy the file to
it.</p>
<p dir="auto">The build makes its own picotool, with USB support, so you can also skip
all that and just do <code>make flash</code>, which builds and flashes the board in
<code>board.local</code>.
<code>make flash-split</code> does the other one.</p>
<div class="markdown-heading" dir="auto"><h3 tabindex="-1" class="heading-element" dir="auto">Tools outside the tree</h3><a id="user-content-tools-outside-the-tree" class="anchor" aria-label="Permalink: Tools outside the tree" href="#tools-outside-the-tree"><svg data-component="Octicon" class="octicon octicon-link" viewBox="0 0 16 16" version="1.1" width="16" height="16" aria-hidden="true"><path d="m7.775 3.275 1.25-1.25a3.5 3.5 0 1 1 4.95 4.95l-2.5 2.5a3.5 3.5 0 0 1-4.95 0 .751.751 0 0 1 .018-1.042.751.751 0 0 1 1.042-.018 1.998 1.998 0 0 0 2.83 0l2.5-2.5a2.002 2.002 0 0 0-2.83-2.83l-1.25 1.25a.751.751 0 0 1-1.042-.018.751.751 0 0 1-.018-1.042Zm-4.69 9.64a1.998 1.998 0 0 0 2.83 0l1.25-1.25a.751.751 0 0 1 1.042.018.751.751 0 0 1 .018 1.042l-1.25 1.25a3.5 3.5 0 1 1-4.95-4.95l2.5-2.5a3.5 3.5 0 0 1 4.95 0 .751.751 0 0 1-.018 1.042.751.751 0 0 1-1.042.018 1.998 1.998 0 0 0-2.83 0l-2.5 2.5a1.998 1.998 0 0 0 0 2.83Z"></path></svg></a></div>
<p dir="auto">Two tools stay outside the tree, and each has a make target that
sets it up once per machine.  Both say what they are missing, and
running either again is safe.</p>
<p dir="auto"><code>make probe-rs</code> builds probe-rs, which programs and debugs the nRF54
radio through the pedal, from <code>~/src/probe-rs</code> into <code>~/bin/probe-rs</code>.
It needs cargo and the libudev development files (<code>systemd-devel</code> on
Fedora).</p>
<p dir="auto"><code>make build123d</code> makes a python venv in <code>~/.build123d</code> for the
3D-printed case in <code>Hardware/Models</code>, and two commands in <code>~/bin</code> that
use it: <code>build123d Compact.py</code> runs the model, and <code>ocp-viewer</code> is
the viewer it draws in, at <a href="http://localhost:3939" rel="nofollow">http://localhost:3939</a>.</p>
<div class="markdown-heading" dir="auto"><h3 tabindex="-1" class="heading-element" dir="auto">Talking to the pedal without root</h3><a id="user-content-talking-to-the-pedal-without-root" class="anchor" aria-label="Permalink: Talking to the pedal without root" href="#talking-to-the-pedal-without-root"><svg data-component="Octicon" class="octicon octicon-link" viewBox="0 0 16 16" version="1.1" width="16" height="16" aria-hidden="true"><path d="m7.775 3.275 1.25-1.25a3.5 3.5 0 1 1 4.95 4.95l-2.5 2.5a3.5 3.5 0 0 1-4.95 0 .751.751 0 0 1 .018-1.042.751.751 0 0 1 1.042-.018 1.998 1.998 0 0 0 2.83 0l2.5-2.5a2.002 2.002 0 0 0-2.83-2.83l-1.25 1.25a.751.751 0 0 1-1.042-.018.751.751 0 0 1-.018-1.042Zm-4.69 9.64a1.998 1.998 0 0 0 2.83 0l1.25-1.25a.751.751 0 0 1 1.042.018.751.751 0 0 1 .018 1.042l-1.25 1.25a3.5 3.5 0 1 1-4.95-4.95l2.5-2.5a3.5 3.5 0 0 1 4.95 0 .751.751 0 0 1-.018 1.042.751.751 0 0 1-1.042.018 1.998 1.998 0 0 0-2.83 0l-2.5 2.5a1.998 1.998 0 0 0 0 2.83Z"></path></svg></a></div>
<p dir="auto">picotool and probe-rs open the pedal's USB device directly, and without
a udev rule only root can.  This is <code>/etc/udev/rules.d/99-pedal.rules</code>:</p>
<div class="snippet-clipboard-content notranslate position-relative overflow-auto" data-snippet-clipboard-copy-content="ATTR{idVendor}=="2e8a", MODE="0660", GROUP="dialout"
ATTR{idVendor}=="ffff", ATTR{idProduct}=="0003", MODE="0660", GROUP="dialout""><pre class="notranslate"><code>ATTR{idVendor}=="2e8a", MODE="0660", GROUP="dialout"
ATTR{idVendor}=="ffff", ATTR{idProduct}=="0003", MODE="0660", GROUP="dialout"
</code></pre></div>
<p dir="auto">The first line covers anything with Raspberry Pi's vendor id, which is
how a board in BOOTSEL shows up; the second is the running pedal, whose
CMSIS-DAP interface is what probe-rs uses for the radio.  You have to be
in the <code>dialout</code> group, and <code>udevadm control --reload</code> as root plus a
replug picks the rule up.  USB audio and MIDI need no rule.</p>
<p dir="auto">The pedal's debug console is <code>/dev/ttyACM0</code>, which needs a kernel with
<code>CONFIG_USB_ACM</code>.  Every distribution kernel has it; a kernel you
configured yourself may not.</p>
<div class="markdown-heading" dir="auto"><h3 tabindex="-1" class="heading-element" dir="auto">Testing</h3><a id="user-content-testing" class="anchor" aria-label="Permalink: Testing" href="#testing"><svg data-component="Octicon" class="octicon octicon-link" viewBox="0 0 16 16" version="1.1" width="16" height="16" aria-hidden="true"><path d="m7.775 3.275 1.25-1.25a3.5 3.5 0 1 1 4.95 4.95l-2.5 2.5a3.5 3.5 0 0 1-4.95 0 .751.751 0 0 1 .018-1.042.751.751 0 0 1 1.042-.018 1.998 1.998 0 0 0 2.83 0l2.5-2.5a2.002 2.002 0 0 0-2.83-2.83l-1.25 1.25a.751.751 0 0 1-1.042-.018.751.751 0 0 1-.018-1.042Zm-4.69 9.64a1.998 1.998 0 0 0 2.83 0l1.25-1.25a.751.751 0 0 1 1.042.018.751.751 0 0 1 .018 1.042l-1.25 1.25a3.5 3.5 0 1 1-4.95-4.95l2.5-2.5a3.5 3.5 0 0 1 4.95 0 .751.751 0 0 1-.018 1.042.751.751 0 0 1-1.042.018 1.998 1.998 0 0 0-2.83 0l-2.5 2.5a1.998 1.998 0 0 0 0 2.83Z"></path></svg></a></div>
<p dir="auto"><code>Validation</code> has the test suite, and it's split by what it needs.</p>
<p dir="auto"><code>make check</code> needs gcc and numpy (<code>python3-numpy</code>), plus node if
you want the web app's tests too; without node those are skipped.  The
bench scripts that talk to a pedal want more: alsa-utils, ffmpeg, scipy
and matplotlib, ngspice for the circuit comparisons, and dbus-python and
PyGObject for Bluetooth MIDI.  On Fedora,</p>
<div class="snippet-clipboard-content notranslate position-relative overflow-auto" data-snippet-clipboard-copy-content="dnf install python3-numpy nodejs alsa-utils ffmpeg-free psmisc \
    python3-scipy python3-matplotlib ngspice python3-dbus python3-gobject"><pre class="notranslate"><code>dnf install python3-numpy nodejs alsa-utils ffmpeg-free psmisc \
    python3-scipy python3-matplotlib ngspice python3-dbus python3-gobject
</code></pre></div>
<p dir="auto"><code>make check</code> runs the part that needs no hardware at all: the MIDI
packetiser, whether the web app still loads and still draws the right
conclusions, and a sweep that asks every biquad in the pedal where it
actually landed.  <code>make check-biquad</code> is that last one on its own, and
<code>make check-effects</code> puts signals through the effects themselves.</p>
<p dir="auto">That last one works because of <code>Validation/bench</code>, which builds the
pedal's actual audio core - the same <code>single_sample()</code>, the same effect
headers, the same compiler flags - as a program on your machine that
takes float samples on stdin and hands them back on stdout.  It is not a
model of the signal path.  It's the signal path, with the two register
blocks the audio core touches replaced by ordinary memory.</p>
<p dir="auto"><code>make check-analysis</code> is the other host-only one, and it is what keeps
the per-effect pages under <code>Documentation/effects</code> honest: every curve on
those pages is a measurement, and this re-measures and says when one has
stopped being true.  It is separate from <code>check</code> because it re-runs
every sweep on every page, which is slow.</p>
<p dir="auto">Then there are the ones that want hardware: <code>make check-hw</code> with a
signal generator, <code>make check-analog</code> with a patch cable from the
pedal's output back to its own input, <code>make check-bench</code> to ask whether
a real board agrees with the host build, <code>make check-hwtone</code> to sweep
the tone stack the codec runs in its own biquads, and <code>make check-loop</code>
if you have two pedals to patch into each other.</p>
<div class="markdown-heading" dir="auto"><h2 tabindex="-1" class="heading-element" dir="auto">Hardware</h2><a id="user-content-hardware" class="anchor" aria-label="Permalink: Hardware" href="#hardware"><svg data-component="Octicon" class="octicon octicon-link" viewBox="0 0 16 16" version="1.1" width="16" height="16" aria-hidden="true"><path d="m7.775 3.275 1.25-1.25a3.5 3.5 0 1 1 4.95 4.95l-2.5 2.5a3.5 3.5 0 0 1-4.95 0 .751.751 0 0 1 .018-1.042.751.751 0 0 1 1.042-.018 1.998 1.998 0 0 0 2.83 0l2.5-2.5a2.002 2.002 0 0 0-2.83-2.83l-1.25 1.25a.751.751 0 0 1-1.042-.018.751.751 0 0 1-.018-1.042Zm-4.69 9.64a1.998 1.998 0 0 0 2.83 0l1.25-1.25a.751.751 0 0 1 1.042.018.751.751 0 0 1 .018 1.042l-1.25 1.25a3.5 3.5 0 1 1-4.95-4.95l2.5-2.5a3.5 3.5 0 0 1 4.95 0 .751.751 0 0 1-.018 1.042.751.751 0 0 1-1.042.018 1.998 1.998 0 0 0-2.83 0l-2.5 2.5a1.998 1.998 0 0 0 0 2.83Z"></path></svg></a></div>
<p dir="auto">The kicad design files (and some supporting infrastructure, like the 3D
printed insert and the enclosure drill rules) are in the <code>Hardware</code>
subdirectory.</p>
<p dir="auto">These days it's just the one board.  <code>Hardware/usb-stomp</code> has the RP2354A
and the TI TAC5242 codec sitting directly on it, and that's the whole
pedal: no cable, no daughtercards, no connectors in between.</p>
<p dir="auto">What's on it:</p>
<ul dir="auto">
<li>a 1/4" input jack and a 1/4" output jack</li>
<li>a third 1/4" jack for an expression pedal or a remote stomp switch</li>
<li>MIDI in and out, on 3.5mm "Type A" TRS jacks (out through a 5V
buffer, in through an optocoupler, like MIDI has always wanted)</li>
<li>USB-C, and the usual 9V guitar pedal power jack</li>
<li>one rotary encoder with a switch under it, and one stomp switch</li>
<li>three addressable WS2812B LEDs</li>
</ul>
<p dir="auto">The MIDI jacks and the expression jack are the genuinely new things.  The
older boards had nowhere to put them - the expression jack in particular
wants two ADC pins, and those are exactly the pins the old MCU board was
spending on hardware MIDI, so it could not have existed there at all.</p>
<p dir="auto">Fair warning on that expression jack, though: the hardware is done and
the firmware can read it, but only when the host asks it to over SysEx.
Right now it's a probe for figuring out what people actually plug in
there - expression pedals don't even agree on which contact is the wiper</p>
<ul dir="auto">
<li>and nothing is wired up to <em>do</em> anything with the result yet.</li>
</ul>
<div class="markdown-heading" dir="auto"><h3 tabindex="-1" class="heading-element" dir="auto">How it used to be</h3><a id="user-content-how-it-used-to-be" class="anchor" aria-label="Permalink: How it used to be" href="#how-it-used-to-be"><svg data-component="Octicon" class="octicon octicon-link" viewBox="0 0 16 16" version="1.1" width="16" height="16" aria-hidden="true"><path d="m7.775 3.275 1.25-1.25a3.5 3.5 0 1 1 4.95 4.95l-2.5 2.5a3.5 3.5 0 0 1-4.95 0 .751.751 0 0 1 .018-1.042.751.751 0 0 1 1.042-.018 1.998 1.998 0 0 0 2.83 0l2.5-2.5a2.002 2.002 0 0 0-2.83-2.83l-1.25 1.25a.751.751 0 0 1-1.042-.018.751.751 0 0 1-.018-1.042Zm-4.69 9.64a1.998 1.998 0 0 0 2.83 0l1.25-1.25a.751.751 0 0 1 1.042.018.751.751 0 0 1 .018 1.042l-1.25 1.25a3.5 3.5 0 1 1-4.95-4.95l2.5-2.5a3.5 3.5 0 0 1 4.95 0 .751.751 0 0 1-.018 1.042.751.751 0 0 1-1.042.018 1.998 1.998 0 0 0-2.83 0l-2.5 2.5a1.998 1.998 0 0 0 0 2.83Z"></path></svg></a></div>
<p dir="auto">It used to be modular, and those board files are all still here.  There
were two little daughtercards for the "core" hardware - the RP2354
microcontroller (<code>Hardware/rp2354</code>) and the TI TAC5112 codec
(<code>Hardware/codec</code>) - plus a board for the audio and 9V DC power jacks
(<code>Hardware/audio-jacks</code>), and a main board (<code>Hardware/pedal-board</code>) for
the pedal IO: i2c connector for the screen, USB-C programming port,
rotary encoders, pin header for stomp switches.  The two halves were
joined by a 12P 0.5mm FFC cable carrying power and data lines (i2c for
control, i2s for audio).</p>
<p dir="auto">That was mostly so I could try out different form factors.  It let me lay
the two halves out independently, and it was flexible enough to cram a
125B enclosure full of jacks, rotaries and the screen all in one top
area.  There was also a worry about noise isolation, which in the end
never had to be tested.</p>
<p dir="auto">I used the nice HiRose BM28 series connectors on the modular boards.
They are absolutely tiny, which makes for a great board footprint but
admittedly also makes for a slightly more complicated board due to the
tiny 0.35mm pitch.  I'm not a fan of the traditional pin headers simply
because they make it so hard to do compact form factors.</p>
<p dir="auto">Those boards are finished and they still work - the firmware builds for
them, and they're still useful for testing.  But what this section used
to say was that if you know what you want, you should just put the codec
directly on the audio jack board and the rp2354 on the IO board.  Which,
yes.  That's the board above.</p>
<div class="markdown-heading" dir="auto"><h3 tabindex="-1" class="heading-element" dir="auto">Images</h3><a id="user-content-images" class="anchor" aria-label="Permalink: Images" href="#images"><svg data-component="Octicon" class="octicon octicon-link" viewBox="0 0 16 16" version="1.1" width="16" height="16" aria-hidden="true"><path d="m7.775 3.275 1.25-1.25a3.5 3.5 0 1 1 4.95 4.95l-2.5 2.5a3.5 3.5 0 0 1-4.95 0 .751.751 0 0 1 .018-1.042.751.751 0 0 1 1.042-.018 1.998 1.998 0 0 0 2.83 0l2.5-2.5a2.002 2.002 0 0 0-2.83-2.83l-1.25 1.25a.751.751 0 0 1-1.042-.018.751.751 0 0 1-.018-1.042Zm-4.69 9.64a1.998 1.998 0 0 0 2.83 0l1.25-1.25a.751.751 0 0 1 1.042.018.751.751 0 0 1 .018 1.042l-1.25 1.25a3.5 3.5 0 1 1-4.95-4.95l2.5-2.5a3.5 3.5 0 0 1 4.95 0 .751.751 0 0 1-.018 1.042.751.751 0 0 1-1.042.018 1.998 1.998 0 0 0-2.83 0l-2.5 2.5a1.998 1.998 0 0 0 0 2.83Z"></path></svg></a></div>
<p dir="auto"><a target="_blank" rel="noopener noreferrer" href="/torvalds/GuitarPedal/blob/main/Images/unified.jpg"><img src="/torvalds/GuitarPedal/raw/main/Images/unified.jpg" alt="The unified board" style="max-width: 100%;"></a></p>
<p dir="auto">The bare <code>usb-stomp</code> board, powered up.</p>
<div class="markdown-heading" dir="auto"><h2 tabindex="-1" class="heading-element" dir="auto">Basic UI</h2><a id="user-content-basic-ui" class="anchor" aria-label="Permalink: Basic UI" href="#basic-ui"><svg data-component="Octicon" class="octicon octicon-link" viewBox="0 0 16 16" version="1.1" width="16" height="16" aria-hidden="true"><path d="m7.775 3.275 1.25-1.25a3.5 3.5 0 1 1 4.95 4.95l-2.5 2.5a3.5 3.5 0 0 1-4.95 0 .751.751 0 0 1 .018-1.042.751.751 0 0 1 1.042-.018 1.998 1.998 0 0 0 2.83 0l2.5-2.5a2.002 2.002 0 0 0-2.83-2.83l-1.25 1.25a.751.751 0 0 1-1.042-.018.751.751 0 0 1-.018-1.042Zm-4.69 9.64a1.998 1.998 0 0 0 2.83 0l1.25-1.25a.751.751 0 0 1 1.042.018.751.751 0 0 1 .018 1.042l-1.25 1.25a3.5 3.5 0 1 1-4.95-4.95l2.5-2.5a3.5 3.5 0 0 1 4.95 0 .751.751 0 0 1-.018 1.042.751.751 0 0 1-1.042.018 1.998 1.998 0 0 0-2.83 0l-2.5 2.5a1.998 1.998 0 0 0 0 2.83Z"></path></svg></a></div>
<p dir="auto">There's no screen.  The pedal has one knob, one footswitch and three
LEDs, and everything else happens in a browser.</p>
<div class="markdown-heading" dir="auto"><h3 tabindex="-1" class="heading-element" dir="auto">On the pedal</h3><a id="user-content-on-the-pedal" class="anchor" aria-label="Permalink: On the pedal" href="#on-the-pedal"><svg data-component="Octicon" class="octicon octicon-link" viewBox="0 0 16 16" version="1.1" width="16" height="16" aria-hidden="true"><path d="m7.775 3.275 1.25-1.25a3.5 3.5 0 1 1 4.95 4.95l-2.5 2.5a3.5 3.5 0 0 1-4.95 0 .751.751 0 0 1 .018-1.042.751.751 0 0 1 1.042-.018 1.998 1.998 0 0 0 2.83 0l2.5-2.5a2.002 2.002 0 0 0-2.83-2.83l-1.25 1.25a.751.751 0 0 1-1.042-.018.751.751 0 0 1-.018-1.042Zm-4.69 9.64a1.998 1.998 0 0 0 2.83 0l1.25-1.25a.751.751 0 0 1 1.042.018.751.751 0 0 1 .018 1.042l-1.25 1.25a3.5 3.5 0 1 1-4.95-4.95l2.5-2.5a3.5 3.5 0 0 1 4.95 0 .751.751 0 0 1-.018 1.042.751.751 0 0 1-1.042.018 1.998 1.998 0 0 0-2.83 0l-2.5 2.5a1.998 1.998 0 0 0 0 2.83Z"></path></svg></a></div>
<p dir="auto">Out of the box the footswitch is bypass - tap for in-circuit or not, hold
it for the tuner - and the knob is the master volume, with either kind of
press on it putting the volume back where it started.  That last one
sounds trivial and isn't: it's the way back when you can't see anything.</p>
<p dir="auto">But none of that is compiled in.  There are five gestures - turn the
knob, tap it, hold it, tap the switch, hold the switch - and what each
one means is a table the pedal looks up and the app writes.  You can
point the knob at any parameter of any effect, or make a single press
take one effect's mix up while it takes another's down.  A pedal with no
screen can't tell you what its knob is for, so that has to be settable
from something that can.</p>
<p dir="auto">The three LEDs, left to right: something is wrong (red for clipping,
amber for dropped samples), in circuit or bypassed, and the chain is
busy - where "busy" means whatever the effect thinks it means, so the
gate lights it while it's gating and the compressor while it's
compressing.</p>
<div class="markdown-heading" dir="auto"><h3 tabindex="-1" class="heading-element" dir="auto">In the browser</h3><a id="user-content-in-the-browser" class="anchor" aria-label="Permalink: In the browser" href="#in-the-browser"><svg data-component="Octicon" class="octicon octicon-link" viewBox="0 0 16 16" version="1.1" width="16" height="16" aria-hidden="true"><path d="m7.775 3.275 1.25-1.25a3.5 3.5 0 1 1 4.95 4.95l-2.5 2.5a3.5 3.5 0 0 1-4.95 0 .751.751 0 0 1 .018-1.042.751.751 0 0 1 1.042-.018 1.998 1.998 0 0 0 2.83 0l2.5-2.5a2.002 2.002 0 0 0-2.83-2.83l-1.25 1.25a.751.751 0 0 1-1.042-.018.751.751 0 0 1-.018-1.042Zm-4.69 9.64a1.998 1.998 0 0 0 2.83 0l1.25-1.25a.751.751 0 0 1 1.042.018.751.751 0 0 1 .018 1.042l-1.25 1.25a3.5 3.5 0 1 1-4.95-4.95l2.5-2.5a3.5 3.5 0 0 1 4.95 0 .751.751 0 0 1-.018 1.042.751.751 0 0 1-1.042.018 1.998 1.998 0 0 0-2.83 0l-2.5 2.5a1.998 1.998 0 0 0 0 2.83Z"></path></svg></a></div>
<p dir="auto"><code>WebMIDI</code> is a static web page that talks to the pedal over USB
MIDI.  There's nothing to install and it runs off a phone.</p>
<p dir="auto">It also talks to the pedal over Bluetooth MIDI.  On Linux, Chrome only
offers Bluetooth to a page with
<code>chrome://flags/#enable-experimental-web-platform-features</code> turned on;
USB needs nothing.</p>
<p dir="auto">It doesn't know what the effects are.  It asks.  The pedal describes
every effect it has - every pot, the ranges, the units, the hover text -
and the app builds itself out of that, so it can't drift out of step with
the firmware, and adding an effect to the pedal makes it show up in the
app without touching the app.</p>
<p dir="auto">What you actually do there is <em>route</em>.  There are seventeen effects and
none of them are in your signal path until you say so: routing picks
which ones run, and in what order, and the order is yours, because a
boost in front of a delay is a different pedal from a delay in front of a
boost.  Whatever you don't route costs nothing.</p>
<p dir="auto">Pots are mostly just numbers, except where they aren't - the tone stacks,
the parametric EQ and the cab sim draw their actual frequency response,
so you can see the curve instead of inferring it from three knob
positions.</p>
<p dir="auto"><a target="_blank" rel="noopener noreferrer" href="/torvalds/GuitarPedal/blob/main/Images/WebMIDI-screenshot.png"><img src="/torvalds/GuitarPedal/raw/main/Images/WebMIDI-screenshot.png" width="420" alt="The WebMIDI app with a tone control and a tape echo routed" style="max-width: 100%;"></a></p>
<p dir="auto">A tone stack with a 10dB mid bump at 810Hz and a tape echo behind it, and
the fifteen effects that aren't routed sitting at the bottom waiting to
be.  The faint grey line is the phase response.</p>
<p dir="auto">Eight scenes fit in the pedal's own flash.  A scene is a routing plus
everything set inside it, and a MIDI program change recalls one, which is
half of what those MIDI jacks are for: a cheap footswitch can step
between scenes with no computer in sight.</p>
<div class="markdown-heading" dir="auto"><h2 tabindex="-1" class="heading-element" dir="auto">Audio effects</h2><a id="user-content-audio-effects" class="anchor" aria-label="Permalink: Audio effects" href="#audio-effects"><svg data-component="Octicon" class="octicon octicon-link" viewBox="0 0 16 16" version="1.1" width="16" height="16" aria-hidden="true"><path d="m7.775 3.275 1.25-1.25a3.5 3.5 0 1 1 4.95 4.95l-2.5 2.5a3.5 3.5 0 0 1-4.95 0 .751.751 0 0 1 .018-1.042.751.751 0 0 1 1.042-.018 1.998 1.998 0 0 0 2.83 0l2.5-2.5a2.002 2.002 0 0 0-2.83-2.83l-1.25 1.25a.751.751 0 0 1-1.042-.018.751.751 0 0 1-.018-1.042Zm-4.69 9.64a1.998 1.998 0 0 0 2.83 0l1.25-1.25a.751.751 0 0 1 1.042.018.751.751 0 0 1 .018 1.042l-1.25 1.25a3.5 3.5 0 1 1-4.95-4.95l2.5-2.5a3.5 3.5 0 0 1 4.95 0 .751.751 0 0 1-.018 1.042.751.751 0 0 1-1.042.018 1.998 1.998 0 0 0-2.83 0l-2.5 2.5a1.998 1.998 0 0 0 0 2.83Z"></path></svg></a></div>
<p dir="auto">Nineteen of them, plus five that are always there and can't be
unrouted: the <strong>Signal Chain</strong> at the front, which is the input trim, the
noise gate and the master volume
(<a href="/torvalds/GuitarPedal/blob/main/Documentation/effects/signal-chain.md">measured</a>), and behind them the
<strong>Settings</strong>, which is whether the input jack is carrying one channel or
two, the MIDI channel, LED brightness and what the tuner is tuning to,
the <strong>USB Audio</strong>, which is what crosses the wire in each direction, the
<strong>Bluetooth Audio</strong>, which is where audio from a phone joins, how loud it
is and what goes back, on a board with a radio, and the <strong>Expression Jack</strong>, which is what
is plugged into it and where that thing's travel ends.</p>
<p dir="auto">They're listed in the order they run in by default.  This is an overview
and not documentation - the app is the reference, because it gets the
ranges, the units and the hover text from the pedal itself rather than
from anything I typed here.</p>
<ul dir="auto">
<li><strong>Hum Filter</strong> - removes the hum single coils and noisy power put on
the guitar, cutting only the hum's own frequencies, so a clean supply
gets no cuts at all.  Switching it on the first time, or moving the
target, listens for a few seconds with the sound left on, so you hear
the hum go: keep the strings quiet while it does.  It runs ahead of
the noise gate.  It does not reach the high buzz some USB chargers
add, and a power bank is quieter there anyway.</li>
<li><strong>Tone</strong> - bass, mid and treble, with the corner frequencies
adjustable and the mid's Q as well.  There are two of them, so one
can go in front of a distortion and one behind it.</li>
<li><strong>Analog In Tone</strong> and <strong>Analog Out Tone</strong> - the same three bands
again, running in the codec's own biquads rather than in the chain.
They cost the audio core nothing, and they keep the two channels
apart where Tone folds them together.  Routed like anything
else, but drawn at the ends of the chain because that is where they
are: analog is the operative word, and they sit outside everything
USB audio can reach, so a Dry capture has already been through the
input one and a Wet capture has not yet been through the output one.
They need a board whose codec answers on i2c.</li>
<li><strong>Preamp</strong> - a two-stage 12AX7 model, class-A biased with the
asymmetry left in, and a JFET stage after it.</li>
<li><strong>Compressor</strong> - level, ratio, attack, release, and a boost, so it
can also just be a clean boost when that's what you want.  The
threshold reaches low enough to work on a quiet pickup with nothing
in front of it.  <a href="/torvalds/GuitarPedal/blob/main/Documentation/effects/compressor.md">Measured</a>.</li>
<li><strong>Auto-Wah</strong> - an envelope filter that sweeps a resonant filter with
the guitar's pick dynamics, by Jacky Mpoka.  Lowpass mode preserves low-end body while
sweeping harmonics (Mu-Tron III style); Bandpass mode isolates the
resonant peak for classic vocal wah (Crybaby style).  Sweeps up for
funk quack or down for synth sweeps.</li>
<li><strong>Boost</strong>, with distortion.  I like this one.  Others may not.  Set
the boost stupidly high and the level low, and instead of clipping at
the level the signal <em>folds</em> back down, which gives you harmonics
that a soft or hard clipper doesn't.</li>
<li><strong>Klonlike</strong> - the obvious model: 18V charge pump for headroom,
germanium diodes, and the clean/dirty blend that tracks the gain
knob.  Originally by Bryan Leavelle.
<a href="/torvalds/GuitarPedal/blob/main/Documentation/effects/klon.md">Measured</a>.</li>
<li><strong>Rat Sketch</strong> - a ProCo RAT, from the Aion FX Helios clone.  One
op-amp with up to 67dB and several decibels an octave of treble
emphasis inside the feedback, then diodes to ground, then the one
backwards Filter knob.  Three clipping modes, because the pedal has
three.  The op-amp saturates inside its own loop and the diodes are
solved rather than approximated, which is where its second harmonic
comes from.  <a href="/torvalds/GuitarPedal/blob/main/Documentation/effects/rat.md">Measured</a>.</li>
<li><strong>Phaser</strong>, <strong>Flanger</strong> and <strong>Vibrato</strong> - the modulation three.  All
simple, all a delay line and an LFO wearing different hats.</li>
<li><strong>Tape Echo</strong> - the Echo King from Cleveland Music Co, a model of the
Maestro Echoplex tape delays, converted from the Hothouse examples.
All credit to Ricky Sheaves, and blame me for the conversion.</li>
<li><strong>Reverb</strong> - comb filters into allpasses, the traditional way.
<a href="/torvalds/GuitarPedal/blob/main/Documentation/effects/reverb.md">Measured</a>.</li>
<li><strong>Pitch</strong> - not the clever FFT kind.  It walks a delay line faster or
slower than real time in two phases, crossfaded with a sine so the
wrap doesn't click.  So it shifts <em>and</em> delays, and it feeds back into
itself, which makes it a short echo that shifts again on every repeat.
Most natural an octave up, but it does fractions.</li>
<li><strong>Tremolo</strong> - amplitude modulation, several shapes.</li>
<li><strong>Parametric EQ</strong> - five bands, two shelves and three peaks, every one
of them tunable across the whole range.</li>
<li><strong>Frenchie Amp</strong> - a small amp: triode, tone stack, power amp.</li>
<li><strong>Test Tone</strong> - sine, triangle, saw or noise at a known level and
frequency.  It replaces the input rather than adding to it, which is
what lets the pedal measure itself.</li>
<li><strong>Cabinet</strong> - a speaker cone as a moving mass rather than as a filter,
integrated at the sample rate.  Pick one of five cabinets and it knows
the rest of itself; the knobs are how hard the amp drives it, how much
the amp lets its resonance bloom, and where the mic is pointed.</li>
</ul>

Philosophy of the GNU Project

Free software means that the software's users have
freedom. (The issue is not about price.) We developed the GNU
operating system so that users can have freedom in their
computing.

Specifically, free software means users have
the four essential freedoms :
(0) to run the program, (1) to study and change the program in source
code form, (2) to redistribute exact copies, and (3) to distribute
modified versions.

Software differs from material objects—such as chairs,
sandwiches, and gasoline—in that it can be copied and changed
much more easily. These facilities are why software is useful; we
believe a program's users should be free to take advantage of them,
not solely its developer.

The articles in the short list below give an overview of GNU
philosophy. For further reading, please check the menu above, especially

pages.text:
GLFS Project Homepage

Web

LFS

Patches

Hints

SLFS

GLFS

MLFS

ALFS

BLFS

LFS

Home

GLFS Home

News

Download

Support

Advisories

Issues

What is Gaming Linux From Scratch?

Gaming Linux From Scratch, which is based on the BLFS
book , helps you install gaming support software, like Steam or Wine,
on a new x86_64 LFS system.

Depending on what you want to install and its type, you may need Multilib
Linux From Scratch (MLFS).

For Steam, it requires 32-bit software as the core of the client is
32-bit. With Wine, it depends on the build type. You can build for pure
64-bit, which is not recommended, and you can do pure 32-bit, which is
also not recommended. However, there are two WoW64 modes, an older one
and a newer one. WoW64 allows running both 64-bit and 32-bit Windows apps
and games on x86_64. The new WoW64 mode doesn't need any Linux 32-bit
libraries but needs the i686 MinGW-w64 toolchain, which also doesn't need
any Linux 32-bit libraries. The older WoW64 mode on the other hand does
require 32-bit libraries.

In cases where 32-bit libraries are needed, MLFS is a
required prerequisuite for this book. MLFS allows you to build 32-bit
apps and libraries, the libraries being the most important part to get
Steam and pure 32-bit or older WoW64 for Wine to work.

Why would I want a GLFS system?

Installing binary-only software on an LFS system is a contentious topic
in the LFS community. However, a lot of people still want to play games
and use Windows software on their new LFS system. GLFS shows how to go
about it, allowing your LFS system to be a viable gaming platform. If you
don't care about gaming, this book is probably not for you but it still
offers instructions on how to install certain packages for 32-bit on
64-bit. It also offers instructions on how to install libglvnd, NVIDIA,
CUDA, MinGW-w64, and Wine which you may still want to use.

What can I do with my GLFS system?

You will be able to use Steam, play popular games using Vulkan and
OpenGL, use the proprietary NVIDIA driver and CUDA if wanted, and run
Windows software via Wine. For Windows software (through Steam and
Wine), you will be able to convert the Direct3D instructions to Vulkan
for optimal performance.

Read the Book Online

GLFS has different versions that line up with LFS+MLFS+BLFS+SLFS
releases. In the past, GLFS had support for both SysVinit and Systemd,
but now only Systemd is supported. The past versions exist as historical
and educational material.

Current Stable

These are the current stable versions of GLFS that are known to work
with an LFS/MLFS, BLFS, and SLFS stable platform.

GLFS stable, uses MLFS and BLFS stable
links

Development

This is GLFS in its current development state. A lot of effort is made
to ensure that the development version is as stable as can. However, there
can still be problems that can occur. In the past, this was the only way to
read the book online without grabbing a copy or rendering the book
yourself. Because of that, stability was and still is a major concern. Now,
everyone has more options.

GLFS development, uses MLFS and BLFS development
links

Other versions

If you want to see older versions, you can browse all releases here .

Thanks to

Douglas Reno, Rahul Chandra, Thomas Trepl, Xi Ruoyao, and the
GLFS contributors

Matthew Burgess.
